narrative:
The 2018 Philadelphia Phillies arrived with genuine optimism. After years of rebuilding, a young core led by Rhys Hoskins, Jorge Alfaro, and Scott Kingery suggested brighter days were coming. The team burst out of the gate in April, posting a 15-10 record powered by big swings from Hoskins, Aaron Altherr, and a lineup that knew how to inflict damage in the late innings. For a brief, electric moment, Citizens Bank Park felt like it mattered again.

The middle months told a more complicated story. June became a crucible — Adam Morgan surrendered a Jason Heyward grand slam that crushed a winnable game, Seranthony Domínguez gave up a Matt Carpenter home run after the offense had just clawed ahead, and a Daniel Murphy single in Washington sent three runs home in what should have been a statement road series. Yet the Phillies managed a 13-14 June, bruised but functional, with Aaron Altherr's walk-off double against the Cardinals on June 18 standing as proof that the fight hadn't left the clubhouse. July brought a bounceback — a 15-11 record, the team's best month — fueled by steady contributions and Andrew Knapp providing unexpected heroics.

August is where the dream began to quietly dissolve. Seranthony Domínguez, who had been one of baseball's best rookie relievers, started showing cracks — giving up a reviewed-and-overturned Ryan Zimmerman home run that cost a crucial game against Washington. Pat Neshek and Víctor Arano were victimized in tight situations, and the bullpen that had carried this team through summer heat began leaking badly. The offense still had its moments — Carlos Santana's August 29 grand slam was a thunderclap — but the team finished August 13-14, and the window was closing fast.

September delivered the final verdict. An 8-20 collapse, the worst month on the ledger, made the math undeniable. Young relievers like Yacksel Ríos got exposed late in games, the rotation wore down, and the 51-game gap between their best and worst months laid bare the fragility of this roster. At 80-82, the Phillies missed the playoffs — but the foundation was visible enough that nobody in Philadelphia was truly giving up. The conversations had already turned to what the next version of this team might look like.

chapters.title: Opening Day Stumble
chapters.description: A rocky March debut gives way to a hot April as the young Phillies announce themselves with a series of clutch offensive explosions.

chapters.title: April's Promise
chapters.description: Hoskins, Altherr, and Alfaro deliver big moments as Philadelphia charges to a 15-10 April and genuine playoff conversation begins.

chapters.title: June Turbulence
chapters.description: The bullpen springs leaks and rivals deliver gut-punch home runs, but the Phillies scratch and claw to stay near .500 through the summer.

chapters.title: July Resurgence
chapters.description: Philadelphia posts its best month at 15-11, with unexpected contributors like Andrew Knapp keeping the playoff dream alive.

chapters.title: August Unraveling
chapters.description: The bullpen buckles under pressure, giving away late-game leads as the Phillies slip to 13-14 and their margin for error evaporates.

chapters.title: September Collapse
chapters.description: An 8-20 September buries any playoff hope and exposes the roster's depth limitations, closing the book on a frustrating but instructive season.
